title: Olympiad Day 8: Germany shake up the race at the top
summary: The Svanes lead a stunning 2.5–1.5 victory over Uzbekistan as USA, China and the chasing pack close in with three rounds to go. Germany produced the result of the day in the Open section, defeating leaders Uzbekistan 2.5–1.5 to throw the race wide open with just three rounds remaining. The Svane brothers delivered the decisive blows on boards three and four, while Javokhir Sindarov continued his unbeaten run with another victory In the Women’s section, China moved into the sole lead after Kazakhstan and India drew 2–2, with Armenia, Mongolia and Uzbekistan all keeping themselves firmly in contention. Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Ceremonial moves and Presidential debate Three ceremonial moves got the eighth round underway in Samarkand. Kirsan Ilyumzhinov, FIDE President from 1995 to 2018 and an honorary citizen of Samarkand, opened play on board one of the Germany – Uzbekistan match, making the ceremonial first move for Vincent Keymer. Hisham Al Taher, General Secretary of the Asian Chess Federation, replied on behalf of Nodirbek Abdusattorov. The action then moved to the Women’s section, where Benard Wanjala, President of the African Chess Confederation, made the opening move on table 22 for the South African team. At the same time, the EXPO area hosted a different kind of chess event: the FIDE Presidential Debate Q&A. Timur Turlov and Jan Henric Buettner introduced themselves before taking questions from journalists for a full hour, covering a wide range of topics related to the future of FIDE and chess. The third candidate, Wadim Rosenstein, was invited but did not take part in the session. Open section Germany stun Uzbekistan at the top Just when it seemed Uzbekistan were beginning to pull away from the field, Germany produced a stunning 2.5–1.5 victory this afternoon, bringing the leading teams closer together and reopening the race at the top of the standings. The Svane brothers were the heroes for Germany, winning on boards three and four against Nodirbek Yakubboev and Shamsiddin Vokhidov respectively. Their two victories more than compensated for Matthias Bluebaum’s defeat on board two against Javokhir Sindarov, who continued his remarkable unbeaten run with 5.5/7. The final game to finish was on board one, where Nodirbek Abdusattorov had to draw on all his defensive resources to hold Vincent Keymer with the black pieces. Frederik Svane later analysed his victory over Yakubboev in the interview area. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LW5alSr8K_s Uzbekistan’s board-five player Mukhiddin Madaminov followed the action closely from the spectators’ area, keeping a watchful eye on his teammates. Germany captain Jan Gustafsson, meanwhile, remained completely unflustered throughout the match, seemingly more absorbed in the pages of his book than the drama unfolding on the boards. India drops more points, China makes a comeback India were unable to secure the important victory they needed against Azerbaijan, as all four games ended in solid draws. Vidit returned to the lineup on board four, replacing Nihal Sarin after five rounds on the bench. Gukesh, playing on board three, was the only Indian player to create a serious winning chance, but a couple of inaccuracies, combined with excellent defensive technique from his opponent Muradli, allowed the game to finish in a draw. China, meanwhile, desperately needed a win after yesterday’s defeat to get back into the leading pack but faced a difficult opponent in Poland. Ding Liren quickly neutralised Poland’s top player, Jan-Krzysztof Duda, agreeing to a draw on board one. The games on boards three and four also ended in solid draws after around four hours, leaving China with little room for maneuver. The only decisive result was recorded on board two, where Wei Yi (undefeated on 5.5/7) worked his magic again. Sacrifice of the day: Fire on the board Szymon Gumularz – Wei Yi Black is already an exchange up and, more importantly, has two extremely dangerous passed pawns deep in the promotion zone. There are several straightforward ways to win, but Wei Yi chooses the most spectacular 32…Qxf3!!, sacrificing his queen to clear the way for the h2-pawn to promote. After 33.Bxf3 Bxf3 34.Kf2 Rf8!, Black’s threats became impossible to parry. Szymon Gumularz resigned after 35.e4 Bd1+ as 36…h1=Q is unavoidable. Netherlands and Armenia share the points The Netherlands and Armenia drew their match 2–2, missing an opportunity to pick up an extra match point and keep pace with the leaders. Jorden van Foreest was on the winning side of a complicated battle against Robert Hovhannisyan, handing the Armenian his first defeat of the tournament. Shant Sargsyan restored the balance for Armenia by defeating Loek van Wely. After the match, Van Foreest joined Charlize van Zyl in the interviews area, where he shared his thoughts on the match and the Netherlands’ performance. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ewwGzNPEjhA USA close the gap with crushing victory Taking full advantage of the results at the top, the United States of America closed the gap with a convincing 3.5–0.5 victory over a strong Serbian team. With just three rounds remaining, the USA are once again firmly in the mix. On board one, Fabiano Caruana scored his third win of the tournament with a neat tactical blow against Alexey Sarana, while remaining undefeated. Tactic of the day Fabiano Caruana – Alexey Sarana The position, arising from a Najdorf Sicilian with opposite-side castling, is a classic attacking scenario. White has sacrificed the g-pawn, but in return has an open g-file to work with, while Black’s queen is awkwardly placed on h7. Caruana exploited both factors with the powerful 24.Rxg7!. Black has no satisfactory response. In the game, Sarana took the rook with 24…Kxg7. Alternatively, 24…Qxg7 25.Rg1 Qxg1 26.Bxg1 leaves White’s queen heading towards h6 with decisive consequences. After 24…Kxg7 25.Bf5, Black’s queen is trapped, and Caruana went on to convert his material advantage without difficulty. One particularly nice variation is 25…Qh8 26.Qg2+ Kf6 27.Qg5#, finishing the game immediately. additionalSources.title: Every Lesson Counts: FIDE Summit in Samarkand puts chess education at the heart of global development
additionalSources.summary: Policymakers, educators, researchers, chess leaders and social innovators from around the world gathered in Samarkand for the FIDE Summit on Chess in Education, one of the flagship events of the 2026 FIDE Year of Chess in Education. Held during the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad and Congress, the Summit brought together experiences from countries at very different stages of integrating chess into education – from established nationwide programmes to emerging initiatives – around one central idea: chess can be much more than a competitive sport. Used effectively, it can become an accessible educational tool for developing concentration, critical thinking, decision-making, creativity and other skills that extend well beyond the chessboard. The opening segment of the Summit featured addresses by FIDE Interim President Viswanathan Anand, Deputy Minister of Preschool and School Education of the Republic of Uzbekistan Farkhod Bokiyev, and President of the International School Chess Federation Timur Turlov. Chess as a tool for learning Drawing on his experience with chess education programmes in India, Anand recalled an initiative launched around 25 years ago to introduce chess in schools and study its impact on children.  After several years, feedback from teachers suggested that students exposed to chess had become more confident when approaching complex subjects such as mathematics and science. Anand also recalled being struck by the confidence and sophisticated vocabulary of young children participating in the programme. For the five-time World Champion, however, the value of chess education is not limited to measurable academic outcomes. “We shouldn’t lose track of the fact that playing chess is fun,” Anand said. “You can’t take a move back. You have to make a decision. You have to choose a move. You have to critically evaluate yourself. All these skills are taught in a pleasant, fun way through chess,” he said Anand also stressed that there can be no single model for Chess in Education. Drawing on India’s experience, where individual states have their own education policies, he argued that programmes must be adapted to local circumstances while countries continue learning from one another. Uzbekistan: investing in chess means investing in human capital Representing the host country, Farkhod Bokiyev presented Uzbekistan’s efforts to develop chess across preschool and school education. According to figures presented at the Summit, more than 100,000 students, including 70,000 girls, are involved in chess clubs across the country. Specialized chess classes have been established in more than 100 schools, while since 2024 an annual chess championship has also been organised for preschool children aged five to seven. The long-term ambition, Bokiyev explained, is to transform chess from a popular activity into a continuous system of intellectual development – giving children an opportunity to discover the game, identifying talent early and creating conditions for further development. He described chess as a universal language in which knowledge, thinking, hard work and skill matter more than nationality, language or social background. “We consider every investment in chess, first and foremost, an investment in human capital,” Bokiyev said. A child sitting at a chessboard today, he noted, may become tomorrow’s scientist, engineer, entrepreneur or community leader. Building systems that can grow ISCF President Timur Turlov focused on the importance of making educational chess systematic, sustainable and scalable. He pointed to Uzbekistan as an example of a country taking a long-term approach to chess and shared Kazakhstan’s experience of rapidly expanding its own school programme. Turlov said a pilot that began with 42 schools in 2023 has since expanded to around 2,500 schools, alongside extensive teacher training. He highlighted another challenge facing modern education: the increasing difficulty children have maintaining concentration in an environment dominated by smartphones, social media, short-form video and digital entertainment. “Chess is a quite unique subject because it helps kids to slow down, calm down and enjoy concentration,” Turlov said. He stressed that the objective is not necessarily to produce professional chess players. Instead, chess can help children develop skills they can later use as engineers, doctors, developers or in other fields. Turlov also emphasised the accessibility of chess: equipment is relatively inexpensive, the basic rules can be taught widely, and programmes can reach children in both urban and rural areas. During the opening segment, Turlov also announced Donald Rojas Fernández as Vice President of the International School Chess Federation. Recognising impact through education The first part of the Summit also celebrated individuals and organisations already using chess to create educational opportunities. The ISCF Impact Awards recognised initiatives supporting girls through chess and education. Honourees included Karandeep Singh Kapany, Regional Marketing Director for India and South East Asia at Duolingo, for expanding opportunities through the Duolingo Dreamers initiative, and H.E. Dr. Auxillia Mnangagwa, First Lady of Zimbabwe, for advancing opportunities for girls through education and chess. Seven 2026 FIDE Year of Chess in Education Awards followed. John Foley received the Educator of the Year Award; the Catalan Chess Federation received the Presidential Award; Zimbabwe received the Kick-starter Award; the Armenian State Pedagogical Institute received the Academic Vanguard Award; Prof. (Dr.) Achyuta Samanta received the Education Philanthropic Award; the Ministry of Sport of Costa Rica, represented by Donald Rojas Fernández, received the Visionary Opening Move Award; and Freedom Holding Corp., represented by Timur Turlov, received the Chess Capital Award. From discussion to action: Barbados partnership The Summit also translated its discussions into concrete commitments. FIDE, the International School Chess Federation and the Ministry of Educational Transformation of Barbados signed a Memorandum of Understanding aimed at integrating chess into Barbadian schools. The agreement, signed by Viswanathan Anand, Timur Turlov and Barbados Minister of Educational Transformation Hon. Chad Blackman, focuses on cooperation in areas including curriculum integration, teacher training and international competition, with chess used to support skills such as critical thinking and problem-solving. The partnership reflected one of the Summit’s recurring themes: successful Chess in Education programmes require cooperation between chess organisations, governments and educators rather than isolated initiatives. title: José Antonio Carrillo receives broad support to continue at the helm of FIDE Americas
summary: During the 46th World Chess Olympiad, on September 24, continental elections for FIDE Americas (Confederación de Ajedrez de las Américas) were held to elect its President and the members of the new Executive Board. By a vote of 29 to 12, José Antonio Carrillo and his team received broad support from the national federations of the Americas. The new Executive Board is composed as follows: José Antonio Carrillo, President Francisco Cruz Arce, Vice President Erick Hernández, Treasurer Enrique Celi, Secretary Sandy Razark, Member María Enriqueta Velásquez, Member Malcolm Powell, Member This result affirms the continent’s confidence in a leadership team committed to unity, cooperation among federations, and the strengthening of chess in the Americas. This marks the beginning of a new stage of joint work, dialogue, and development, aimed at further driving the growth of chess across the continent.
